title: JD Vance Calls H-1B Visa Programme 'Completely Broken,' Backs Scrapping It
excerpt: The vice president said he would support eliminating the H-1B system, days after a second federal judge blocked the administration's $100,000 visa fee and an executive order tightened scrutiny of sponsoring firms.
body:
• U.S. Vice President JD Vance said he would support eliminating the H-1B visa programme, calling it "completely broken."
  • Two federal judges have now blocked the administration's $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions, ruling the government skipped required rule-making procedures.
  • What this means for you: if you are an H-1B holder or applicant, the $100,000 fee cannot currently be enforced while the court battles continue, but the administration is tightening scrutiny of sponsoring firms — including checking whether they recently laid off comparable U.S. workers — so keep documentation of your role's salary level and specialization.
  • The remarks landed days after a September 18 executive order directing immigration officials to scrutinise layoffs at sponsoring firms and weight H-1B selection toward higher salaries.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said he would back eliminating the H-1B visa programme entirely, describing the system as "completely broken" and accusing employers of misusing it to replace American workers with cheaper foreign labour.

Vance made the remarks in an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec aboard Air Force Two that aired last Thursday on Human Events Daily. "My view is the H-1B programme is completely broken, and I'd be very supportive of just eliminating it," he said. "But while we have it, what we have to do is protect American workers."

He said the programme had been "totally taken advantage of" by technology companies and accounting firms.

"If you're going to bring in an accountant making $45,000 a year to replace an accountant who is an American making $60,000 a year, that's not you using the programme to bring in a genius. That's you destroying American jobs and defrauding the American people."

— JD Vance, U.S. Vice President

Defending the $100,000 fee

Vance used the interview to defend the administration's most controversial H-1B measure: a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new petitions for workers outside the United States, introduced in September 2025 and extended last month through September 21, 2027. The fee was designed, he said, so that "if you're just trying to replace an American accountant with a cheaper foreign accountant, then you're not going to pay $100,000."

That fee is now blocked. On October 1, U.S. District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland ruled that immigration authorities and the State Department failed to follow required administrative rule-making before imposing it — the second court to halt enforcement, after a federal judge in Boston temporarily stopped it in June. The rulings mean the fee cannot currently be collected while the legal fight continues.

Context and background

The H-1B programme lets U.S. employers hire foreign workers for specialised occupations, capped at 65,000 visas a year plus 20,000 for advanced-degree holders, typically renewable to six years. Indian nationals make up the largest share of beneficiaries — the programme is the primary route by which Indian tech professionals enter the American workforce, and it feeds the green-card backlog that leaves many in limbo for years.

A September 18 directive instructed immigration officials to consider whether sponsoring firms have recently laid off comparable domestic workers, and ordered scrutiny of previously filed labour-condition applications. A tiered selection mechanism prioritises higher-salaried roles. Vance said the administration had "done more on the H-1B visa than any administration in history," but suggested the reforms still fall short of fixing decades of offshoring and globalisation.

Impact and analysis

A sitting vice president openly supporting the programme's elimination raises the ceiling on what Congress and the administration may attempt — from steeper fees to outright caps reductions. The court rulings, however, show the limits of executive action: twice now, judges have found the administration tried to rewrite immigration economics without following its own rule-making procedures.

Even with the fee blocked, firms face layoff audits, wage-tiered selection and labour-condition scrutiny — favouring higher-paid hires and squeezing the lower-wage staffing firms that have long dominated the lottery.

The diaspora angle

Indians dominate H-1B approvals, and tens of thousands of Indian families in the U.S. have built lives around a visa now at the centre of a political fight over its existence. The elimination talk, however remote legislatively, injects fresh uncertainty into renewal decisions, job mobility and the already-glacial green-card queue. Indian IT services firms and American employers of Indian talent will be watching whether Vance's posture becomes policy or remains interview rhetoric.

What's next

The immediate fights are in court: the government will likely appeal both fee rulings or attempt a formal rule-making to reimpose the charge on firmer legal ground. Meanwhile, the September 18 reforms are already in force regardless of the fee's status. The question for the months ahead is whether the administration moves from tightening the programme to legislating its end — and whether Congress, where the tech industry still holds sway, lets that happen.
